lesson.title: Building Atoms from the Ground Up
lesson.summary: The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals available before occupying higher energy ones, giving a predictable subshell filling order that lets you write any atom's ground state electron configuration.
lesson.body:
The word Aufbau comes from German for "building up," and the principle is exactly that: to predict an atom's electron configuration, imagine adding one electron at a time to successively larger atomic numbers, always placing each new electron into the lowest energy orbital that still has room. It is the organizing rule behind every electron configuration you write, turning what could be a memorized list of exceptions into a single, mostly reliable procedure.

The tricky part is that subshell energy does not simply track shell number. In a multi electron atom, inner electrons partially shield outer electrons from the full pull of the nucleus, and that shielding changes the relative energies of subshells in a way that pure shell number does not predict. The result is a filling order that weaves back and forth between shells: 1s, then 2s, then 2p, then 3s, then 3p, then, surprisingly, 4s before 3d, then 4p, then 5s before 4d, then 5p, then 6s before 4f, and so on. A common memory aid is the diagonal rule: write each subshell on a diagonal chart and read off the order by following the arrows, or equivalently, fill in order of increasing n + l, breaking ties by choosing the smaller n first. For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4; for 3d, n + l = 3 + 2 = 5, so 4s fills first.

Potassium is the classic example of why this matters. Potassium has atomic number 19. If you filled shells strictly by n, you might expect the nineteenth electron to enter 3d. It does not. Following the real energy order, the first eighteen electrons fill 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (2+2+6+2+6 = 18, matching argon's configuration), and the nineteenth electron goes into 4s, not 3d, giving potassium the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1. This is exactly why potassium behaves chemically like sodium and lithium, forming plus one ions, rather than behaving like a transition metal: its outermost, most reactive electron sits in an s orbital, not a d orbital.

The Aufbau principle is a very good approximation, not an absolute law, and chemistry students eventually run into its two most famous exceptions among the first row transition metals. Chromium, atomic number 24, is predicted by strict Aufbau to be [Ar] 4s2 3d4, but its actual ground state configuration is [Ar] 4s1 3d5. Copper, atomic number 29, is predicted to be [Ar] 4s2 3d9, but is actually [Ar] 4s1 3d10. In both cases, moving one electron from 4s into 3d creates a half filled (3d5) or completely filled (3d10) d subshell, and the extra stability from having every orbital in that subshell singly or fully occupied, tied to symmetric electron distribution and reduced electron repulsion, outweighs the small energy cost of leaving 4s with only one electron.

These exceptions do not break the Aufbau principle; they show its limits. The rule is a genuinely reliable first pass for the vast majority of elements, and even chromium and copper are still filling the lowest available orbitals in essentially the predicted order, just with one electron nudged over for extra stability. Once you can apply Aufbau confidently, the next two ideas, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule, explain the finer details of exactly how electrons distribute themselves once they arrive in a given subshell.
